newsitem.title: BULGARIA: High rate boosts Bulgarians' T-paper investment.
newsitem.headline: High rate boosts Bulgarians' T-paper investment.

text.p: Some 200 Bulgarians queued up on Wednesday in front of the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) building to buy treasury paper, hoping to profit from the record high 300 percent interest rate set by the BNB.
In a move to stabilise the country's troubled financial system the BNB on Monday raised the interest rate to 300 percent in an attempt to curb inflation and support the weakening national currency.
"The government paper now gives very high yield and seems to be the safest place for our savings," Ivan Petrov, a 59-year old engineer, told Reuters.
Annual yields offered by the Finance Ministry range from 300 percent on three-month T-bills to 343 percent on six-month T-bills and 450 percent on one-year T-bills.
The BNB has placed a total of 14 banks under special supervision since May in a bid to avert their collapse.

Lack of radical market reforms in recent years and unclear and changing economic policies from the socialist government in the past 17 months have put local banks under pressure and caused severe liquidity problems.
Although deposits in those banks were guaranteed by the state, access to them was restricted.
The law provides for a 100 percent state guarantee on personal savings in those banks and 50 percent coverage of companies' deposits.

However, deposits in foreign exchange are paid out either in their lev equivalent or in small portions over six-month periods. Deposits in the last nine banks placed under supervision on Monday will be compensated after the courts rule these banks' solvency.
So far the courts have postponed ruling several times on the first wave of bank closures sought by the central bank in May.
People's savings were additionally eroded by soaring consumer price inflation of 113 percent in the first eight months of the year.
"The dollar has proven to be the safest investment. I would not convert my dollars to buy T-bills. I am investing in treasury paper is some spare levs," said another man in the queue.
Looming bankruptcies and general economic instability have pushed the lev down sharply since the beginning of the year.
"I have no problem with savings. All of my salary is spent on current expenses," said one passer by.
Bulgarians are unlikely to convert their dollar savings into new bank deposits after their negative experience this year, said economists.
The finance ministry said maturity payments in cash on the country's domestic debt will be a problem. Maturity payments in September were covered by new issues of government securities.
Government papers are becoming more like shares in get-rich-quick schemes, said local media.
However, some still believed in the state's trustworthiness.
"The country is in a terrible crisis and by buying government paper I am lending my money and helping the country recover," said one elderly pensioner. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
